title: Part 5, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Raskolnikov had been a vigorous champion of Sonia against Luzhin, despite carrying such a weight of horror and anguish in his own heart. But having endured so much that morning, he found a kind of relief in a change of emotions, apart from the strong personal impulse that drove him to defend Sonia. He was also agitated, especially at certain moments, by the thought of his approaching conversation with Sonia: he had to tell her who killed Lizaveta. He knew the terrible suffering it would cause him, and he kept pushing the thought away. So when he cried out on leaving Katerina Ivanovna's, "Well, Sofya Semyonovna, we shall see what you'll say now!" he was still outwardly excited, still energized and defiant from his victory over Luzhin. But strangely, by the time he reached Sonia's lodging, he felt a sudden helplessness and fear. He stopped at the door, asking himself the strange question: "Do I have to tell her who killed Lizaveta?" It was strange because he knew he couldn't help telling her, and couldn't put it off any longer. He didn't yet know why it had to be done — he only felt it — and the agonizing sense of his powerlessness before the inevitable nearly crushed him. To cut short his hesitation and suffering, he quickly opened the door and looked at Sonia from the doorway. She was sitting with her elbows on the table, her face in her hands, but seeing Raskolnikov she got up at once and came toward him as though she had been expecting him.
"What would have become of me without you?" she said quickly, meeting him in the middle of the room.
Clearly she had been desperate to say this to him. It was what she had been waiting for.
Raskolnikov went to the table and sat down in the chair she had just risen from. She stood facing him, two steps away, exactly as she had the day before.
"Well, Sonia?" he said, feeling his voice tremble. "It was all because of 'your social position and the habits associated with it.' Did you understand that just now?"
Her face showed her distress.
"Just don't talk to me the way you did yesterday," she interrupted. "Please don't start. There's enough misery without that."
She hurried to smile, afraid he might not like the reproach.
"It was silly of me to leave. What's happening there now? I wanted to go back right away, but I kept thinking that... you would come."
He told her that Amalia Ivanovna was throwing them out and that Katerina Ivanovna had run off somewhere "to seek justice."
"My God!" cried Sonia. "Let's go at once..."
She snatched up her cape.
"It's always the same with you!" Raskolnikov said irritably. "You have no thought for anyone but them! Stay with me for a while."
"But... Katerina Ivanovna?"
"You won't miss Katerina Ivanovna, don't worry. She'll come to you on her own since she's run out," he added peevishly. "If she doesn't find you here, you'll be blamed for it..."
Sonia sat down in painful suspense. Raskolnikov was silent, staring at the floor, deliberating.

"This time Luzhin didn't want to prosecute you," he began, not looking at Sonia. "But if he had, if it had suited his plans, he would have sent you to prison — if not for Lebeziatnikov and me. Right?"
"Yes," she agreed in a faint voice. "Yes," she repeated, preoccupied and distressed.
"But I might easily not have been there. And Lebeziatnikov showing up was pure accident."
Sonia was silent.
"And if you'd gone to prison — what then? Do you remember what I said yesterday?"
Again she didn't answer. He waited.

"I thought you'd cry out again, 'Don't say it, stop.'" Raskolnikov gave a laugh, though a forced one. "Still silent?" he asked a minute later. "We have to talk about something, you know. I'd actually like to know how you'd resolve a certain 'problem,' as Lebeziatnikov would put it." He was beginning to lose the thread. "No, really, I'm serious. Imagine, Sonia, that you'd known all of Luzhin's intentions beforehand — known for certain that they would ruin Katerina Ivanovna and the children, and you too — since you don't count yourself — Polenka as well, because she'd end up the same way. Well, what if suddenly it all depended on your decision whether he or they would go on living — whether Luzhin should live and keep doing evil, or Katerina Ivanovna should die? How would you decide which of them should die? That's my question."
Sonia looked at him anxiously. There was something peculiar in this halting question — it seemed to be approaching something in a roundabout way.
"I had a feeling you were going to ask something like that," she said, looking at him searchingly.
"I'm sure you did. But how would you answer it?"
"Why do you ask about something that could never happen?" Sonia said reluctantly.
"So it would be better for Luzhin to go on living and doing evil? You haven't even dared to decide that!"

"But I can't know God's will... And why do you ask what can't be answered? What use are such pointless questions? How could it depend on my decision? Who made me a judge over who should live and who should die?"
"Oh, once you bring God into it, nothing can be done," Raskolnikov grumbled darkly.
"Just say straight out what you want!" Sonia cried in distress. "You're leading up to something again... Did you come here just to torture me?"
She couldn't control herself and burst into bitter tears. He looked at her in gloomy misery. Five minutes passed.

"Of course you're right, Sonia," he said softly at last. He was suddenly changed. His tone of assumed arrogance and helpless defiance was gone. Even his voice had suddenly gone weak. "I told you yesterday I wasn't coming to ask forgiveness, and almost the first thing I've done is ask forgiveness... What I said about Luzhin and Providence — that was for my own sake. I was asking forgiveness, Sonia..."
He tried to smile, but there was something helpless and incomplete in his pale smile. He bowed his head and hid his face in his hands.

And suddenly a strange, startling wave of bitter hatred for Sonia passed through his heart. Alarmed and bewildered by this feeling, he lifted his head and looked intently at her; but he met her anxious, painfully worried eyes fixed on him — there was love in them. His hatred vanished like a phantom. It wasn't the real feeling; he had mistaken one emotion for the other. It only meant that the moment had come.
He hid his face in his hands again and bowed his head. Suddenly he went pale, rose from the chair, looked at Sonia, and without a word sat down mechanically on her bed.
That moment felt terrifyingly similar to the one when he had stood over the old woman with the axe in his hand and felt he must not lose another second.
"What's wrong?" asked Sonia, terribly frightened.

He couldn't speak. This was not at all, not at all how he had planned to tell her, and he didn't understand what was happening to him. She went to him softly, sat down on the bed beside him, and waited, not taking her eyes off him. Her heart pounded and sank. It was unbearable. He turned his deathly pale face toward her. His lips moved, straining helplessly to form words. A wave of terror passed through Sonia's heart.
"What's wrong?" she repeated, drawing back slightly.

"Nothing, Sonia, don't be frightened... It's nonsense. Really, it's all nonsense when you think about it," he muttered, like someone delirious. "Why did I come to torture you?" he added suddenly, looking at her. "Honestly, why? I keep asking myself that, Sonia..."
He had perhaps been asking himself that question fifteen minutes ago, but now he spoke helplessly, barely aware of what he was saying, trembling all over.
"Oh, how you're suffering!" she whispered in distress, looking at him intently.
"It's all nonsense... Listen, Sonia." He suddenly smiled — a pale, helpless smile that lasted two seconds. "You remember what I was going to tell you yesterday?"
Sonia waited uneasily.
"I said as I was leaving that I might be saying goodbye forever, but that if I came today, I would tell you who... who killed Lizaveta."
She began trembling all over.
"Well, I've come to tell you."
"Then you really meant it yesterday?" she whispered with difficulty. "How do you know?" she asked quickly, as if suddenly regaining her senses.
Sonia's face grew paler and paler, and she was breathing with difficulty.
"I know."
She paused for a minute.
"Have they found him?" she asked timidly.
"No."
"Then how do you know about it?" she asked again, barely audibly, after another minute's pause.
He turned to her and looked at her very intently.
"Guess," he said, with the same twisted, helpless smile.
A shudder ran through her.
"But you... why are you frightening me like this?" she said, smiling like a child.

"I must be a very close friend of his... since I know," Raskolnikov continued, still gazing into her face as though unable to look away. "He... didn't mean to kill Lizaveta... He killed her by accident... He meant to kill the old woman while she was alone, and he went there... and then Lizaveta came in... and he killed her too."
Another terrible moment passed. They still stared at each other.
"You can't guess?" he asked suddenly, feeling as though he were throwing himself off a cliff.
"N-no..." whispered Sonia.
"Take a good look."

The moment he said it, the same familiar sensation froze his heart. He looked at her and suddenly seemed to see Lizaveta's face in hers. He clearly remembered Lizaveta's expression when he had approached her with the axe and she had backed against the wall, stretching out her hand with childlike terror in her face — looking the way small children do when something begins to frighten them, staring fixedly and anxiously at whatever scares them, shrinking back and holding out their little hands, on the verge of tears. Almost the same thing was happening now with Sonia. With the same helplessness and the same terror, she gazed at him for a long time. Then suddenly she put out her left hand, pressed her fingers weakly against his chest, and slowly began to rise from the bed, moving further away while keeping her eyes fixed on him even more intensely. Her terror was contagious. The same fear appeared on his face. He stared back at her in almost the same childlike way.
"Have you guessed?" he whispered at last.
"Good God!" An awful wail tore from her chest.

She collapsed helplessly onto the bed, face in the pillows, but a moment later she sat up, moved quickly toward him, seized both his hands, and gripping them tight with her thin fingers, stared into his face again with that same desperate look. In this last, desperate gaze she tried to search him and find some last shred of hope. But there was no hope; there was no doubt left; it was all true. Later, when she recalled that moment, she found it strange that she had seen it all so clearly at once. She couldn't have said, for instance, that she had foreseen something like this — and yet now, the moment he told her, she felt as if she really had foreseen it all along.
"Stop, Sonia, enough! Don't torture me," he begged miserably.
It was not at all, not at all the way he had imagined telling her — but this was how it happened.

She jumped up, seeming not to know what she was doing, and wringing her hands, walked to the middle of the room. But she quickly went back and sat down beside him again, her shoulder almost touching his. Then all at once she flinched as though stabbed, cried out, and fell to her knees before him, not knowing why.
"What have you done — what have you done to yourself?" she cried in despair. She sprang up, threw her arms around his neck, and held him tight.
Raskolnikov pulled back and looked at her with a mournful smile.
"You're a strange girl, Sonia — you kiss me and embrace me when I tell you about that... You don't realize what you're doing."
"There is no one — no one in the whole world now as unhappy as you!" she cried in a frenzy, not hearing his words, and she broke into violent, hysterical weeping.
A feeling long unfamiliar flooded his heart and softened it at once. He didn't fight it. Two tears rose to his eyes and hung on his lashes.
"Then you won't leave me, Sonia?" he said, looking at her almost with hope.
"No, no, never, nowhere!" cried Sonia. "I'll follow you — I'll follow you everywhere! Oh God! How miserable I am!... Why didn't I know you before? Why didn't you come to me sooner? Oh, God!"
"Here I've come."
"Yes, now! What should we do now?... Together, together!" she repeated as if unconsciously, hugging him again. "I'll follow you to Siberia!"
He recoiled, and the same hostile, almost contemptuous smile appeared on his lips.
"Maybe I don't want to go to Siberia yet, Sonia," he said.
Sonia looked at him quickly.

After her first passionate, agonizing sympathy for the unhappy man, the terrible reality of the murder overwhelmed her again. In his changed tone she seemed to hear the murderer speaking. She stared at him in bewilderment. She still knew nothing — why, how, for what purpose. Now all those questions rushed into her mind at once. And again she couldn't believe it: "He — he is a murderer! Is it possible?"

"What does this mean? Where am I?" she said in utter bewilderment, as though unable to come to her senses. "How could you — you, a man like you... How could you bring yourself to it? What does it mean?"
"Oh, to rob her. Stop, Sonia," he answered wearily, almost with irritation.
Sonia stood as if struck dumb, but suddenly she burst out:
"You were hungry! It was... to help your mother? Yes?"
"No, Sonia, no," he muttered, turning away and hanging his head. "I wasn't that hungry... I did want to help my mother, yes, but... that's not the real reason either... Don't torture me, Sonia."
Sonia clasped her hands.

"Can it really be true? Good God, what a truth! Who could believe it? And how could you give away your last kopeck and yet rob and murder? Oh!" she cried suddenly. "That money you gave Katerina Ivanovna... that money. Could it possibly be..."

"No, Sonia," he broke in quickly. "That money wasn't from the robbery. Don't worry! My mother sent it, and it arrived while I was sick — the day I gave it to you... Razumikhin saw it... he received it for me... That money was mine — my own."
Sonia listened in bewilderment, trying her hardest to comprehend.

"And that money... I don't even really know if there was any money," he added softly, as if thinking aloud. "I took a purse from her neck, made of chamois leather... a purse stuffed full of something... but I didn't look inside; I suppose I didn't have time... And the items — chains and trinkets — I buried them under a stone the next morning, in a courtyard off V— Prospect. They're all still there..."
Sonia strained every nerve to listen.
"Then why... you said you did it to rob her, but you didn't take anything?" she asked quickly, grasping at a straw.

"I don't know... I still haven't decided whether to take that money or not," he said, musing again; then, seeming to wake with a start, he gave a brief, bitter smile. "What stupid nonsense I'm talking, right?"
A thought flashed through Sonia's mind: Was he insane? But she dismissed it at once. No, it was something else. She couldn't make sense of any of it.

"You know, Sonia," he said suddenly with conviction, "let me tell you this: if I'd simply killed because I was hungry" — he stressed every word, looking at her intently yet sincerely — "I would be happy now. You have to believe that! What would it matter to you," he cried a moment later with a kind of despair, "what would it matter if I confessed I'd done wrong? What do you gain by such a pointless victory over me? Oh, Sonia, is that why I've come to you today?"
Again Sonia tried to speak but couldn't.
"I asked you to come with me yesterday because you're all I have left."
"Go where?" Sonia asked timidly.

"Not to steal and not to murder — don't worry," he said with a bitter smile. "We're so different... And you know, Sonia, it's only now, only this very moment, that I understand where I was asking you to go yesterday. Yesterday when I said it, I didn't know myself. I asked you for one thing, I came to you for one thing: don't leave me. You won't leave me, Sonia?"
She squeezed his hand.

"And why, why did I tell her? Why did I let her know?" he cried a minute later in despair, looking at her with infinite anguish. "Here you are, expecting me to explain everything, Sonia — you're sitting there waiting for it, I can see that. But what can I tell you? You won't understand, and you'll only suffer — on my account! So you're crying and embracing me again. Why? Because I couldn't bear my burden and came to dump it on someone else: 'You suffer too, and I'll feel better!' Can you really love such a contemptible wretch?"
"But aren't you suffering too?" cried Sonia.
Again the same wave of feeling surged through his heart and for an instant softened it.

"Sonia, I have a wicked heart — remember that. It may explain a great deal. I've come to you because I'm wicked. There are men who wouldn't have come. But I'm a coward and... a contemptible wretch. But... never mind! None of that matters. I need to talk, but I don't know how to begin."
He paused and sank into thought.
"We're so different!" he cried again. "We're nothing alike. And why, why did I come? I'll never forgive myself for it."
"No, no — it was good that you came," cried Sonia. "It's better that I know — far better!"
He looked at her in anguish.
"What if that really was the reason?" he said, as though reaching a conclusion. "Yes, that's what it was! I wanted to become a Napoleon — that's why I killed her... Do you understand now?"
"N-no," Sonia whispered naively and timidly. "Only keep talking, keep talking — I'll understand, I'll understand it inside myself!" she begged.
"You'll understand? All right, we'll see!" He paused and was lost in thought for some time.

"It was like this: one day I asked myself a question — what if Napoleon, for instance, had been in my place, and if instead of Toulon and Egypt and the crossing of Mont Blanc to launch his career, there had simply been some ridiculous old hag, a pawnbroker, who had to be murdered to get money from her trunk — for his career, you understand. Well, would he have gone through with it if there'd been no other way? Wouldn't he have felt a pang that it was so far from glorious and... sinful, too? Well, I have to tell you that I tormented myself over that question for a terribly long time, and I was deeply ashamed when I finally guessed — all at once, somehow — that not only would it not have given him the slightest pang, it wouldn't even have occurred to him that it wasn't glorious... that he wouldn't have seen anything to hesitate over, and that if there'd been no other way, he'd have strangled her in a second without a thought! So I too... stopped thinking about it... and killed her, following his example. And that's exactly how it was! You think it's funny? Yes, Sonia, the funniest thing of all is that maybe that's precisely how it happened."
Sonia didn't find it funny at all.
"You'd better tell me straight out... without examples," she begged, even more timidly and almost inaudibly.
He turned to her, looked at her sadly, and took her hands.

"You're right again, Sonia. Of course it's all nonsense — practically just talk! You know my mother has almost nothing. My sister happened to get a good education and was condemned to drudgery as a governess. All their hopes rested on me. I was a student, but I couldn't support myself at the university and had to leave for a while. Even if I'd scraped by like that, in ten or twelve years I might, with luck, hope to become some kind of teacher or clerk with a salary of a thousand rubles" — he recited it as though from memory — "and by then my mother would have been worn out with worry and grief, and I still couldn't have kept her comfortable, while my sister... well, my sister might have fared even worse! It's a bitter thing to spend your whole life passing everything by, turning your back on everything, forgetting your mother, and meekly swallowing the insults heaped on your sister. Why should you? Just to bury them and then burden yourself with a wife and children — only to leave them penniless too? So I decided to take the old woman's money and use it for my first years without burdening my mother — to support myself through university and for a little while after — and to do it all on a grand, thorough scale, to build a completely new career and start a new, independent life... Well... of course, killing the old woman was wrong... Well, enough of that."
He dragged himself to the end of his speech in exhaustion and let his head sink.
"Oh, that's not it, that's not it," Sonia cried in distress. "How could anyone... no, that's not right, not right."
"You can see for yourself it's not right. But I've told you the truth — it is the truth."
"As if that could be the truth! God!"
"I only killed a louse, Sonia — a useless, loathsome, harmful creature."
"A human being — a louse!"

"I know she wasn't a louse," he answered, looking at her strangely. "But I'm talking nonsense, Sonia," he added. "I've been talking nonsense for a long time... That's not it — you're right about that. There were completely different reasons for it! I haven't talked to anyone in so long, Sonia... My head aches terribly now."

His eyes burned with feverish brilliance. He was nearly delirious; a restless smile hovered on his lips. His terrible exhaustion showed through his agitation. Sonia could see how he was suffering. Her own head was spinning too. And he spoke so strangely — it seemed almost comprehensible, and yet... "But how? How? God!" She wrung her hands in despair.

"No, Sonia, that's not it," he began again suddenly, lifting his head as though struck by a new and sudden train of thought. "That's not it! Better... imagine — yes, this is definitely better — imagine that I'm vain, envious, malicious, petty, vindictive and... well, perhaps with a tendency toward insanity. Let's get it all out at once! I know they've already been talking about madness — I noticed. I just told you I couldn't support myself at the university. But you know what? Maybe I could have. My mother would have sent me what I needed for the fees, and I could have earned enough for clothes, boots, and food. Tutoring jobs came up at half a ruble each. Razumikhin manages! But I turned sulky and wouldn't do it. Yes, sulky — that's the right word! I sat in my room like a spider. You've been to my room — you've seen it... Do you know, Sonia, that low ceilings and tiny rooms crush the soul and the mind? Oh, how I hated that garret! And yet I refused to leave it — I wouldn't, on principle! I went days without going out, wouldn't work, wouldn't even eat. If Nastasya brought me something, I ate it; if she didn't, I went all day without — I wouldn't ask, out of sheer stubbornness! At night I had no light; I lay in the dark and wouldn't earn money for candles. I should have been studying, but I sold my books; the dust lies an inch thick on the notebooks on my table. I preferred lying still and thinking. And I had dreams all the time — strange dreams of every sort, no need to describe them! But then I began to imagine that... No, that's not it! Again I'm telling it wrong! You see, I kept asking myself: why am I so stupid that when others are stupid — and I know they are — I won't be smarter? Then I understood, Sonia, that if you wait for everyone to get smarter, it'll take too long... Afterward I realized it would never happen — that people won't change, that nobody can change them, and it's not worth the effort. Yes, that's right. That's the law of their nature, Sonia, that's how it is!... And I know now that whoever is strong in mind and spirit will have power over them. Whoever dares the most is the most right in their eyes. Whoever scorns the most will be their lawgiver, and whoever dares the most will be most in the right! That's how it's always been, and that's how it will always be. You'd have to be blind not to see it!"

Though Raskolnikov was looking at Sonia as he said this, he no longer cared whether she understood or not. The fever had taken complete hold of him; he was in a kind of gloomy ecstasy — he really had gone too long without talking to anyone. Sonia sensed that his dark creed had become his faith and his code.

"I realized then, Sonia," he went on eagerly, "that power is given only to the person who dares to stoop down and pick it up. There's only one thing needed: you just have to dare! Then for the first time in my life, an idea took shape that no one had ever thought of before me. No one! I saw as clear as day how strange it is that not a single person in this insane world has ever had the courage to just grab it all and send it to hell! I... I wanted to have that courage... and I killed her. I only wanted to dare, Sonia! That was the whole reason!"
"Oh, stop, stop!" cried Sonia, clasping her hands. "You turned away from God, and God has struck you down — given you over to the devil!"
"So Sonia, when I used to lie there in the dark and all of this became clear to me — was that the devil tempting me?"
"Stop! Don't laugh, blasphemer! You don't understand — you don't understand! Oh God! He won't understand!"

"Quiet, Sonia! I'm not laughing. I know myself that it was the devil leading me. Quiet, Sonia, quiet!" he repeated with grim insistence. "I know all this — I've thought it over and over, whispered it all to myself lying there in the dark... I've argued every point with myself, and I know it all! And how sick I was of going over it again and again! I kept wanting to forget it all and start fresh, Sonia, and stop thinking. And you mustn't suppose I rushed into it like a fool. I went into it like a wise man — and that was precisely my undoing. And you mustn't suppose, for instance, that I didn't know that if I started questioning whether I had the right to seize power, I obviously didn't have it — or that if I asked myself whether a human being is a louse, it proved she wasn't one, at least not for me, though she might be for someone who would go straight to his goal without asking questions... If I agonized all those days over whether Napoleon would have done it or not, I clearly sensed that I wasn't Napoleon. I had to endure the full torment of that battle of ideas, Sonia, and I longed to throw it off: I wanted to murder without theorizing, to murder for my own sake, for myself alone! I didn't want to lie about it even to myself. It wasn't to help my mother that I killed — that's nonsense. I didn't kill to get wealth and power so I could become a benefactor of mankind. Nonsense! I simply did it — I killed for myself, for myself alone, and whether I later became a benefactor to others or spent my life like a spider catching people in my web and sucking the life out of them, I couldn't have cared less at that moment... And it wasn't the money I wanted, Sonia, when I did it. It wasn't so much the money as something else... I understand all of this now... Understand me! Perhaps I'd never have committed another murder. I needed to find out something else; something else was driving me. I needed to find out, and find out quickly, whether I was a louse like everyone else or a man. Whether I could step over the line or not. Whether I dared to stoop down and pick up power, or not. Whether I was a trembling creature, or whether I had the right..."
"The right to kill? The right to kill?" Sonia clasped her hands.

"Oh, Sonia!" he cried irritably, and seemed about to retort, but fell into contemptuous silence. "Don't interrupt me, Sonia. I want to prove just one thing: that the devil led me on, and afterward showed me I had no right to take that path, because I'm just as much a louse as everyone else. He was mocking me, and here I've come to you now! Welcome your guest! If I weren't a louse, would I have come to you? Listen: when I went to the old woman's that day, I only went to try it... You can be sure of that!"
"And you murdered her!"

"But how did I murder her? Is that how people commit murder? Do people go to kill the way I went? Someday I'll tell you how I went! Did I murder the old woman? I murdered myself, not her! I destroyed myself in one blow, once and for all... But it was the devil who killed that old woman — not me. Enough, enough, Sonia! Let me be!" he cried in a sudden spasm of agony. "Let me be!"
He pressed his elbows to his knees and squeezed his head in his hands like a vise.
"What suffering!" A wail of anguish tore from Sonia.
"Well, what should I do now?" he asked, suddenly raising his head and looking at her with a face hideously distorted by despair.

"What should you do?" she cried, jumping up. Her eyes, which had been full of tears, suddenly blazed. "Stand up!" She seized him by the shoulder; he got up, looking at her almost in bewilderment. "Go at once, right now — stand at the crossroads, bow down, and first kiss the earth you've defiled. Then bow down to the whole world, to all four sides, and say out loud to everyone: 'I am a murderer!' Then God will give you life again. Will you go? Will you go?" she asked, trembling all over, seizing both his hands, squeezing them tight, and gazing at him with eyes full of fire.
He was stunned by her sudden fervor.
"You mean Siberia, Sonia? I have to give myself up?" he asked gloomily.
"Accept suffering and redeem yourself through it — that's what you must do."
"No! I'm not going to them, Sonia!"

"But how will you go on living? What will you live for?" cried Sonia. "How is that possible now? How can you face your mother? Oh, what will become of them! But what am I saying? You've already abandoned your mother and sister. You have abandoned them already! Oh God!" she cried. "He knows all this himself. How can he live like this — how? What will become of you?"

"Don't be a child, Sonia," he said softly. "What harm have I done them? Why should I go to the authorities? What would I tell them? It's all a phantom... They destroy millions of people themselves and consider it a virtue. They're rogues and scoundrels, Sonia! I'm not going to them. And what would I say? That I killed her but didn't dare take the money and hid it under a stone?" he added with a bitter smile. "They'd laugh at me and call me a fool for not keeping it. A coward and a fool! They wouldn't understand, and they don't deserve to understand. Why should I go? I won't. Don't be a child, Sonia..."
"You won't be able to bear it — it will be too much!" she repeated, stretching out her hands in desperate supplication.
"Maybe I've been too hard on myself," he observed gloomily, lost in thought. "Maybe after all I am a man and not a louse, and I've been too quick to condemn myself. I'll make another fight for it."
A haughty smile appeared on his lips.
"What a burden to carry! And for your whole life, your whole life!"
"I'll get used to it," he said grimly and thoughtfully. "Listen," he began a minute later. "Stop crying — it's time to talk about facts. I've come to tell you the police are after me, on my trail..."
"Oh!" Sonia cried in terror.

"Why are you crying out? You want me to go to Siberia, yet now you're scared? But listen: I'm not going to turn myself in. I'll fight it, and they won't get anywhere. They have no real evidence. Yesterday I was in grave danger and thought I was lost, but today things look better. Everything they have can be read two ways — I can turn their accusations to my advantage, do you understand? And I will, because I've learned my lesson. But they'll certainly arrest me. If not for something that happened, they would have arrested me today for sure; maybe they still will today... But it doesn't matter, Sonia. They'll let me go again — because they have no real proof, and there won't be any, I give you my word. They can't convict on what they've got. Enough... I just wanted you to know... I'll try to manage things with my mother and sister so they won't be frightened... My sister's future is secure now, I believe... and my mother's should be too... Well, that's all. Be careful, though. Will you come to see me in prison?"
"Oh, I will! I will!"

They sat side by side, mournful and dejected, as though they'd been cast up by a storm, alone on some deserted shore. He looked at Sonia and felt how enormous her love for him was — and strangely, he suddenly felt it as a weight, a pain, to be loved so much. Yes, it was a strange and terrible sensation! On his way to Sonia he had felt that all his hopes rested on her; he had expected to unload at least part of his suffering. But now, when her whole heart turned toward him, he suddenly felt himself immeasurably more unhappy than before.
"Sonia," he said, "maybe you'd better not come to see me in prison."
Sonia didn't answer; she was crying. Several minutes passed.
"Do you have a cross?" she asked, as though suddenly remembering.
At first he didn't understand the question.

"No, of course not. Here, take this one — it's cypress wood. I have another, a copper one that belonged to Lizaveta. I exchanged with Lizaveta: she gave me her cross and I gave her my little icon. I'll wear Lizaveta's now and give you this one. Take it... it's mine! It's mine, you know," she begged. "We'll go to suffer together, and together we'll bear our cross!"
"Give it to me," said Raskolnikov.
He didn't want to hurt her feelings. But he immediately drew back the hand he'd reached out for the cross.
"Not now, Sonia. Later," he added to comfort her.
"Yes, yes, that's better," she repeated with conviction. "When you go to face your suffering, put it on then. You'll come to me, I'll put it on you, we'll pray together, and then we'll go."
At that moment someone knocked three times at the door.
"Sofya Semyonovna, may I come in?" came a very familiar and courteous voice.
Sonia rushed to the door in alarm. The fair-haired head of Mr. Lebeziatnikov appeared in the doorway.
